patterns.name: BFS for Unweighted Shortest Path
patterns.explanation: BFS visits nodes in order of distance from the source on an unweighted graph. The first time a node is reached is by the shortest path. Multi-source BFS solves 'distance to nearest of several sources' in one pass.
patterns.when_to_use: Shortest path in unweighted graph, word ladder, rotting oranges, walls and gates, 01-matrix, open the lock, shortest bridge, jump game IV.
patterns.intuition: BFS expands a frontier one layer at a time. Distance from source equals BFS layer at which the node is discovered.
common_pitfalls: Forgetting the visited set — duplicates and exponential blowup
Tracking distance per node instead of per layer (subtle off-by-one)
Using BFS on weighted graphs (wrong)
Not enqueuing all sources at the start when the problem is multi-source

patterns.name: DFS for Connectivity & Components
patterns.explanation: DFS marks reachable nodes from a start. Repeated DFS from each unvisited node enumerates connected components (undirected) or strongly connected components (with extra machinery).
patterns.when_to_use: Number of Islands, Number of Connected Components in Undirected Graph, Surrounded Regions, Pacific Atlantic Water Flow, Friend Circles, Flood Fill.
patterns.intuition: From any unvisited node, a DFS explores its entire component. Counting how many DFS launches you do = number of components.
common_pitfalls: Recursive DFS on huge grids → stack overflow (use iterative)
Forgetting to mark visited before recursing
Confusing component count with cycle count
Treating directed graphs as undirected and miscounting

patterns.name: Topological Sort
patterns.explanation: Linear ordering of vertices such that every directed edge u→v has u before v. Two algorithms: Kahn's (BFS over zero-in-degree nodes) and DFS-based (postorder reversed). Both detect cycles as a side effect.
patterns.when_to_use: Course Schedule (I, II), Alien Dictionary, Sequence Reconstruction, Sort Items by Groups Respecting Dependencies, Parallel Courses, Build Order.
patterns.intuition: A DAG has a 'water-flow' direction; topological sort linearizes it. Kahn's algorithm peels off zero-indegree nodes; if the graph isn't fully consumed, there's a cycle.
common_pitfalls: Forgetting cycle detection — algorithm silently produces wrong order
DFS-based topo: pushing on entry instead of exit
Tie-breaking lexicographically when not requested (or vice versa)
Using on undirected graphs (undefined)

patterns.name: Union-Find (DSU)
patterns.explanation: Disjoint-Set Union: maintain a forest where each tree represents a set. `find` walks to the root (with path compression); `union` attaches one root to another (with union by rank/size). Near-O(1) amortized.
patterns.when_to_use: Number of Connected Components, Redundant Connection, Accounts Merge, Friend Circles, Smallest String With Swaps, Most Stones Removed With Same Row or Column, Earliest Moment When Everyone Become Friends.
patterns.intuition: DSU answers 'are u and v in the same set?' and 'merge their sets' incrementally — useful when edges arrive online or when you need to query connectivity at multiple points in time.
common_pitfalls: Forgetting path compression and union by rank — gets O(N) per op
Storing parents as a Map instead of array when keys aren't dense
Mutating during iteration
Trying to *split* a union (DSU only supports merges)
patterns.complexity_signature: Near O(α(N)) per op, effectively O(1)

patterns.name: Dijkstra's Algorithm
patterns.explanation: Single-source shortest path on a graph with non-negative edge weights. A min-heap pulls out the closest unvisited node; relax each outgoing edge.
patterns.when_to_use: Network Delay Time, Cheapest Flights Within K Stops (with state extension), Path with Minimum Effort, Swim in Rising Water, Minimum Cost to Make at Least One Valid Path. Any non-negative weighted shortest-path problem.
patterns.intuition: If all weights are non-negative, the closest unvisited node has its final distance settled — relaxing it can only update farther nodes. The heap orders this 'closest unvisited' query in O(log V).
common_pitfalls: Using on graphs with negative edges (incorrect)
Decrease-key not implemented — accept the lazy-delete pattern (push duplicates, skip stale)
Missing the 'skip if popped distance > known' check
Confusing edges with nodes in the priority queue tuple
patterns.complexity_signature: O((V + E) log V) with binary heap

patterns.name: Bellman–Ford & Negative Cycles
patterns.explanation: V−1 rounds of relaxing every edge. Detects negative cycles in a final extra round. Slower than Dijkstra but handles negative weights and is simpler to reason about.
patterns.when_to_use: Cheapest Flights Within K Stops (limited-edge variant), arbitrage detection (negative log of FX rates), find shortest path with at most K edges. Whenever Dijkstra cannot apply due to negative weights.
patterns.intuition: After V−1 relaxation rounds, all shortest paths (with V vertices) have been found, since any simple path has ≤ V−1 edges. A V-th round that still relaxes proves a negative cycle.
common_pitfalls: Stopping early when no relaxation happens (correct optimization but easy to forget)
Confusing 'reachable from a negative cycle' with 'on a negative cycle'
Using Bellman–Ford when Dijkstra would suffice (unnecessarily slow)
Off-by-one in 'at most K edges' (number of relaxation rounds)

patterns.name: Minimum Spanning Tree (Prim / Kruskal)
patterns.explanation: Two algorithms for MST: Prim grows the tree from a seed using a min-heap of crossing edges; Kruskal sorts all edges and unions endpoints with DSU, accepting an edge iff it connects two components.
patterns.when_to_use: Min Cost to Connect All Points, Optimize Water Distribution in a Village, Connecting Cities with Minimum Cost. Whenever you need 'cheapest set of edges that connects all nodes'.
patterns.intuition: MST is the lightest acyclic spanning subgraph. The cut property guarantees that the lightest edge crossing any cut belongs to *some* MST. Prim and Kruskal are two ways of incrementally honoring this property.
common_pitfalls: Building the wrong adjacency representation (Kruskal only needs edge list; Prim needs adjacency)
Forgetting cycle prevention (DSU union returning false)
Allowing duplicate edges and double-counting
Implementing Prim with O(V²) when O(E log V) is required
patterns.complexity_signature: Kruskal: O(E log E). Prim: O((V+E) log V).

patterns.name: Cycles & Strongly Connected Components
patterns.explanation: Cycle detection: in directed graphs via DFS coloring (WHITE/GRAY/BLACK), in undirected graphs via DFS-with-parent or DSU. SCCs via Tarjan (one DFS with low-links) or Kosaraju (two DFS passes).
patterns.when_to_use: Detect cycles (Course Schedule), Critical Connections in a Network (bridges via Tarjan), Strongly Connected Components, Find Eventual Safe States.
patterns.intuition: GRAY-on-GRAY in directed DFS = back edge = cycle. SCCs partition a directed graph into maximal mutually-reachable groups; Tarjan/Kosaraju find them in O(V+E).
common_pitfalls: Using two-color DFS in directed graph (insufficient — must distinguish in-progress)
Confusing bridges with articulation points (related but not the same)
Implementing Tarjan from memory and getting low-link wrong
Treating undirected as directed (or vice versa) for cycle detection
